About: Probe Energy vs. Resolvable Size

Concept
Resolving a detail of size d needs a probe of momentum p ≳ ħ/d, so the minimum probe energy Emin = pc = ħc/d climbs as d shrinks. One cursor drives two locked log rulers — size down, energy up.
Serves
Explain how higher momenta can probe shorter distances.
Inquiry
Drag from a human hair down to the quark limit and count decades: nine decades of size cost nine decades of energy.
Misconception
"A better lens could see smaller." Resolution is set by the probe's wavelength, not the lens; only higher momentum shortens that wavelength.
PrincipleIn this sim
Predict firstThe guided-inquiry cards ask for a commitment before each reveal; the zoom that tests a prediction runs only after a choice.
Misconception encodedThe "better lens" choice freezes a dashed ghost wave at the old wavelength while the target shrinks 1000× — it visibly cannot resolve it.
Invariant visibleħc ≈ 0.197 GeV·fm ties the size ruler to the energy ruler at every zoom; E and p read identically (E = pc).
Operational readoutsd, Emin and the imaging-technology chip update live off one cursor; p = Emin/c is restated in The Physics sheet.
Formal layer on demandThe de Broglie relation, the 197 GeV example and a live worked run open from the ⚛︎ The Physics button.
Model honestyThe probe is treated as massless (E = pc) in the target's rest frame, and the wave is drawn with period ƛ = λ/2π.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The resolution ladder

Here’s our big question: how small can physics resolve, and at what energy cost? On screen you’ll see a person, size d, with the probe wave that just resolves it. The bottom ruler runs from everyday sizes toward the smallest things physics can resolve.

2 · The price of 1000×

Let’s start zooming. Every probe is a wave, and detail finer than about one wavelength blurs away. From here, d will drop 1000×. What do you think must happen to the minimum probe energy Emin?

3 · Where light gives up

Now we’re down at d = 100 nm — a virus. Visible light has a wavelength of around 400–700 nm. Why do you think a light microscope can no longer resolve this target?

4 · Decades for decades

Let’s keep going. At d = 10⁻¹⁰ m we’re at the size of an atom, and the proton is about five orders of magnitude smaller (1.7 fm). How do you think Emin must change to resolve the proton?

5 · Why no one has seen a quark

One last stop: d = 10⁻¹⁸ m — quark scale. Why do you think no microscope will ever photograph a quark?

And that’s the whole story in one line: nine decades of size cost nine decades of energy — d·Emin never leaves ħc ≈ 0.197 GeV·fm.

The Physics

Resolution and probe energy · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim zooms from the size of the Earth down to below a quark and shows, at each size d, the smallest probe energy Emin it assigns to that size. Every instrument, from the eye to the Large Hadron Collider, is chosen by how small a detail it must resolve.

What you'll learn

  • How the probe wave in the stage relates to the size d you want to resolve.
  • How a probe's momentum and energy depend on its wavelength.
  • How Emin changes as d runs through 27 decades of size.
  • Which kinds of instrument the sim assigns to which sizes.
The layout: a probe wave, a target of size d, and two rulers that share one cursor.

What's on screen

  • Probe wave (coloured wave): five periods across the view. Its colour follows the probe type.
  • Target (centre): an object of size d, one fifth of the stage wide, with its name and size on a pill beneath.
  • Pills (top): d on the left, and "min. probe: …" with a colour dot on the right.
  • Ruler band (bottom): the size ruler with its coloured technology strip, and the probe-energy ruler.
  • Cursor (accent diamond): the current d, drawn on both rulers at once.
See itPut the cursor at your current d. Watch for: the cursor crossing both rulers at once, with d and Emin given as numbers.

Fixed: the probe is treated as massless, like a photon, and energies are quoted in the target's rest frame. The sim's technology bands are its own markers, not a model of forces.

03

Detail finer than the wave is lost

A wave can only report features about as big as its own wavelength or bigger. The sim turns this into a rule of thumb: the wave must wiggle at least once across the target.

Left: a wave whose period matches the target. Right: a much longer wave, dashed as the sim draws its "ghost" wave. Each period is drawn as ƛ, which is λ/2π.
  • The probe wave in the stage is drawn with period ƛ = λ/2π, the reduced wavelength. The true wavelength λ is 2π ≈ 6.3 times longer.
  • The sim's rule is ƛ ≲ d. It is an order-of-magnitude criterion, not a sharp cut-off.
  • When ƛ is far larger than d, the wave is nearly uniform across the target and cannot tell it from a point.
  • A better lens does not change this. A lens focuses and magnifies the wave, but it cannot bring back detail the wave never carried.
See itZoom in by three decades while the probe stays the same. Watch for: the dashed ghost wave keeping its long wavelength while the target shrinks, with a label saying one wave is much larger than the view.
04

A shorter wave carries more momentum

The reduced wavelength is tied to momentum by ƛ = λ/2π = ħ/p. Putting this into the rule ƛ ≲ d gives a floor on the probe's momentum:

A massless probe, like a photon, has E = pc. The floor on momentum becomes a floor on energy:

  • The constant is ħc = 0.19733 GeV·fm, which is also 197.33 eV·nm.
  • Worked example, d = 1 nm: Emin = 197.33 eV·nm ÷ 1 nm = 197 eV. In the sim this is an X-ray.
  • This Emin is a minimum. Any probe with this momentum or more can resolve d.
See itGo to d = 1 nm. Watch for: Emin reading 197 eV and the "min. probe" pill reading X-ray.
05

Size and energy move decade for decade

Because Emin = ħc/d, the product of the two is a constant. Divide d by any factor and Emin is multiplied by that same factor:

  • On the rulers, one decade of size lines up with one decade of energy. The 27 decades of d on the size ruler cover 27 decades of Emin, about 2 feV to 2 TeV.
  • From the opening size, d = 1.7 m gives 116 neV. A target 1000 times smaller, 1.7 mm, needs 1000 times more: 116 µeV.
The sim's two locked rulers, with the cursor at d = 1.70 m. One zoom of 1000 times in size is 1000 times in energy.
d Emin

See itZoom in by three decades. Watch for: Emin climbing by a factor of 1000 as d falls by 1000, with the cursor on both rulers.
06

The minimum energy is a floor, not a beam energy

Emin is the momentum the probe must deliver, written as an energy through E = pc. The sim quotes it as a momentum transfer in the target's rest frame, not as the energy of a beam.

Same momentum, two different bills. The sim always quotes the first line.
  • A probe with mass m and the same p has kinetic energy K = √((pc)² + (mc²)²) − mc², which is (pc)²/2mc² when pc ≪ mc².
  • At d = 1 nm, pc = 197.3 eV. A photon needs 197 eV. An electron with the same momentum has K = 38 meV, about 5000 times less.
  • It is also a floor in another sense. Real lenses resolve about λ/2 = πƛ, roughly 3ƛ, so a working instrument needs more than the sim's minimum.
See itGo to d = 0.1 nm, an atom, where Emin = 1.97 keV. Watch for: the pill reading X-ray while the technology readout says electron microscope.
07

Where each technology takes over

The coloured strip on the size ruler marks which family of instruments the sim assigns to each size. Each edge is the sim's own marker.

The sim's four bands, with the smallest Emin each has to cover.
  • Naked eye to about 70 µm, a hair's width. Visible light is not the limit here; the eye's own optics are.
  • Light microscope to about 105 nm, where Emin = 1.88 eV lies inside the visible range, 1.65–3.27 eV. Real optical microscopes reach about 200 nm.
  • Electron microscope to about 40 pm, where Emin = 4.9 keV, a floor that an electron meets with far less energy.
  • Accelerator · collider below that. At 10⁻¹⁸ m, Emin = 197 GeV. Colliders do not form an image; they reconstruct the debris of collisions.
See itGo to d = 10⁻¹⁸ m. Watch for: Emin reading 197 GeV and the "min. probe" pill reading collider beam.
08

Where it matters

  • Electron microscopes. A 100 keV electron has a wavelength of about 3.7 pm. Conventional instruments resolve about 0.1 nm, limited by lens aberrations rather than by the wave.
  • Sizes of nuclei and the proton. In the 1950s Robert Hofstadter scattered electrons of a few hundred MeV at Stanford and measured the sizes of nuclei and of the proton (Nobel Prize 1961). The sim puts the proton at 1.7 fm, where Emin = 116 MeV.
  • Quarks inside the proton. Electrons of 7–20 GeV scattered at SLAC in the late 1960s revealed point-like constituents. Hard collisions at the LHC exchange momenta of a TeV, about 2 × 10⁻¹⁹ m in the sim's relation.
Go deeper: beating the limit without a shorter wave
  • Super-resolution fluorescence microscopy (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2014) images detail well below λ/2 with visible light. It gains extra information by controlling which molecules emit, not by shortening the wave.
  • The sim's rule is about what a plain, one-shot wave can resolve. It does not cover tricks that add information.
09

Summary

In one line. To resolve a detail of size d, the probe's wavelength must be about d or shorter, which costs at least Emin = ħc/d: make d ten times smaller and the energy floor rises ten times.

Key points

  • The sim's rule is ƛ ≲ d, an order-of-magnitude criterion.
  • With ƛ = ħ/p and E = pc, it gives Emin = ħc/d.
  • Each decade of size costs one decade of energy.
  • Emin is a floor, not a beam energy.

Common mix-ups

  • "A better lens or a brighter beam lets you see smaller." The wavelength sets the limit. Brightness only adds signal.
  • "Emin = 197 GeV means a 197 GeV machine." Emin is a momentum, written as an energy. A massive probe with that momentum carries less kinetic energy.
  • "The wave drawn in the stage has wavelength d." It is drawn with period ƛ = d. The true wavelength is λ = 2πƛ, about 6.3 times longer.

Things to try on your own

  • Set d to 10 nm and then to 100 pm. Predict Emin from ħc = 197.3 eV·nm, then check the readout.
  • Drag along the ruler band to the green-to-cyan edge and read Emin.
  • Move the Emin slider to about 100 MeV and read which object d now matches.
